questions.prompt: A single company looks attractive on its own. What first move best reduces one-company tunnel vision?
choices: Set it beside an alternative claim on capital so opportunity cost becomes visible.
Judge it fully in isolation because comparison adds unnecessary distraction.
Accept the initial valuation as complete once the company appears attractive.
questions.explanation: Paired comparison reduces one-company tunnel vision because valuation changes when it is set beside an alternative claim on capital. Opportunity cost becomes visible through comparison.

questions.prompt: Two real-estate names share a sector label. What question should come before treating their risk as equal?
choices: Whether the labels are similar enough to make the investment character the same.
Whether leverage, assets, earnings stability, and management differ inside the sector.
Whether the sector label alone makes structure and finances irrelevant.
questions.explanation: Similar industry labels do not create equal risk. Structure and finances can diverge sharply because leverage, assets, earnings stability, and management differ within a sector.

questions.prompt: A superior business trades at a large premium over a weaker peer. Which test protects against overpaying for quality?
choices: Assume the better company is always the better stock because quality settles the decision.
Ignore the premium because business superiority cannot be overcapitalized by price.
Ask whether the premium exceeds the value of the quality difference.
questions.explanation: A superior business may still be overpriced relative to a weaker peer when the premium exceeds the value of the quality difference. Price can overcapitalize quality.

questions.prompt: A peer has the lower multiple in a pair. What should be checked before calling it the better value?
choices: Whether the lower multiple alone identifies the better purchase.
Whether weaker balance sheets or cyclical exposure justify the discount.
Whether cheapness can replace any need to explain the business condition.
questions.explanation: A low-priced peer may be cheap for valid reasons. Weaker balance sheets or cyclical exposure may justify a discount, so cheapness must be explained.

questions.prompt: McGraw Edison and McGraw-Hill share overlapping words. What should control appraisal instead of name similarity?
choices: The overlapping words, because similar names imply similar investment merits.
Name familiarity, because business differences matter less when names resemble each other.
Business economics, because the companies represent different businesses despite similar names.
questions.explanation: McGraw Edison and McGraw-Hill name similarity is irrelevant to valuation because they represent different businesses despite overlapping words. Business economics control appraisal.

questions.prompt: A stable-growth company earns a premium valuation. Which limit should keep the premium from becoming automatic?
choices: Paying too high a multiple can consume the benefit of stability and lower expected return.
Stable growth deserves unlimited valuation because stability removes price risk.
Expected return rises as price rises whenever growth appears stable.
questions.explanation: Growth stability earns a premium only up to a point. Paying too high a multiple can consume the benefit of stability because expected return falls as price rises.

questions.prompt: A market favorite commands a premium over its pair. What skeptical question should guide the comparison?
choices: How popular is the favorite, since popularity itself proves the premium is deserved?
How quickly can the favorite be accepted without testing the advantage behind the premium?
What concrete advantage justifies the premium, if any?
questions.explanation: Pair analysis trains skepticism toward market favorites by asking what concrete advantage justifies the premium. Popularity is evidence to test, not accept.

questions.prompt: A cyclical company looks cheap using current earnings. What adjustment best protects the pair comparison?
choices: Use normalized earnings because peak or trough results can distort relative cheapness.
Use current earnings only because cycle position does not affect the denominator.
Treat trough results as permanent because cyclicality removes the need for interpretation.
questions.explanation: Cyclical companies need normalized earnings in pair comparisons because peak or trough results can distort relative cheapness. Cycle position changes the denominator.

questions.prompt: A table of pairs shows one company with the lower ratio. What is the right way to use that signal?
choices: Treat the lower ratio as a formula that automatically identifies the buy.
Use the ratio as a judgment tool whose value depends on inputs and business interpretation.
Ignore business context because ratios require no interpretation once a pair is listed.
questions.explanation: A table of pairs is a tool for judgment, not a formula. Final appraisal depends on the quality of the inputs and business interpretation because ratios require context.

cards.front: How does paired comparison reduce one-company tunnel vision?
cards.back: It sets a valuation beside an alternative claim on capital. That comparison makes opportunity cost visible and prevents judging a company as though isolation were enough.

cards.front: Why do similar industry labels fail to create equal risk?
cards.back: Companies inside a sector can differ in leverage, assets, earnings stability, and management. Structure and finances can diverge sharply even when the industry label looks similar.

cards.front: Why can a superior business still be overpriced relative to a weaker peer?
cards.back: The premium can exceed the value of the quality difference. A better company is not automatically a better stock because price can overcapitalize quality.

cards.front: Why might a low-priced peer be cheap for valid reasons?
cards.back: A discount may be justified by weaker balance sheets or cyclical exposure. The lower multiple member of a pair is not automatically better because cheapness must be explained.

cards.front: Why is McGraw Edison and McGraw-Hill name similarity irrelevant to valuation?
cards.back: McGraw Edison and McGraw-Hill represent different businesses despite overlapping words. Similar names do not imply similar investment merits because business economics control appraisal.

cards.front: Why does growth stability earn a premium only up to a point?
cards.back: Paying too high a multiple can consume the benefit of stability. Stable growth does not deserve unlimited valuation because expected return falls as price rises.

cards.front: How does pair analysis train skepticism toward market favorites?
cards.back: It asks what concrete advantage justifies the premium. A market favorite does not deserve its premium by definition because popularity is evidence to test, not accept.
